Name: Hard coal, burned in power plant
Description: The module describes the operation of an average plant in the region. The plant is used for middle load with 4000 hours of operation at full capacity per year. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of main characteristics (LHV, sulphur and ash content of coal, efficiency of the plant) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, particles, mercury) a bottom-up approach has been used and supplemented by typical emission factors in cases of data gaps (based on EEA/EPA). CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions have been derived from fuel types (from IEA data) and IPCC emission factors. Airborne emission data has been updated for 2019, whereas other inputs and outputs come from the original dataset. The dataset consists on the collection of information about single plants. Base data on all major power plants in 2019 have been integrated, to the extent possible. The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Emissions of trace substances (except for mercury) were derived from emission factors in the literature (EEA/EPA). The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air. The share of the recycled ash is country-specific. For the disposal of the remaining ash, typical country-specific compositions are taken into account in appropriate disposal modules. Name: Electricity, hard coal, at power plant
Description: The dataset describes the electricity production at an average hard coal power plant at busbar in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The datasets includes as only input the fuel use. The corresponding dataset describing the combustion of the fuel contains the following data, assumptions, and extrapolations: The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of some of the main characteristics (efficiency and capacity of the plant, capacity factor) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, mercury, and CO2) a bottom-up approach has been used, based upon the complete set of these factors for every US hard coal power stations in 2004. The limited number of combined heat and power plants has not been included in the analysis. All other emission data are based on US EPA (1998) and US DOE (1998) reports. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The amounts of retained SOx (due to use of FGD) and retained NOx (due to use of SCR) have been calculated as the difference between uncontrolled average US SOx and NOx emissions in year 1998 and actual region specific SOx and NOx emissions in year 2004 assuming that the characteristics of the coals have not changed in the meanwhile. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. The share of the recycled ash is the average US. For the disposal of the remaining ash, the German disposal dataset has been used, roughly representing average European environmental impacts due to hard coal ash disposal.; UUID: 2a6fe7c3-39ac-3307-8327-e77f98fa9b7b includedProcesses:Conversion of hard coal into electricity: electricity output at busbar. The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Name: Hard coal, burned in power plant
Description: The dataset describes the operation of an average hard coal power plant in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of some of the main characteristics (efficiency and capacity of the plant, capacity factor) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, mercury, and CO2) a bottom-up approach has been used, based upon the complete set of these factors for every US hard coal power stations in 2004. The limited number of combined heat and power plants has not been included in the analysis. All other emission data are based on US EPA (1998) and US DOE (1998) reports. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The amounts of retained SOx (due to use of FGD) and retained NOx (due to use of SCR) have been calculated as the difference between uncontrolled average US SOx and NOx emissions in year 1998 and actual region specific SOx and NOx emissions in year 2004 assuming that the characteristics of the coals have not changed in the meanwhile. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. The share of the recycled ash is the average US. For the disposal of the remaining ash, the German disposal dataset has been used, roughly representing average European environmental impacts due to hard coal ash disposal.; UUID: 3cdf3954-947a-33b0-8a80-2286c75caf38 includedProcesses:Energy conversion for electricity production. Use of fuel oil for startup is accounted for. Particle removal is included in this module. DeSOx and DeNOx are described in different modules. The relevant SOx and NOx retention amounts have been estimated for this region with a top-down approach. SOx and NOx emissions are those finally released to air. It is assumed that 25% of the plants are river cooled, 75% use cooling towers (guestimate: same share as for European hard coal power plants). The water treatment is described in separate modules. Material requirements of cooling water, chemicals, etc, as well as wastes produced during operation are assumed to be the same as for European hard coal power plants. The amount of recycled ash is the US average. The disposal of non-recycled ashes is modelled using the German disposal dataset as approximation (it roughly exhibits average environmental impacts among the other country-specific European datasets for ash disposal). The hard coal fuel use per MJin is region specific, depending on the heating value of the consumed coal. Transport means and average distances for supply of hard coal to the modelled power plant are US averages. Power plant infrastructure is included by a mix of 100 MW and 500 MW units, whose share reproduces the average power plant capacity in this region with the simplifying assumption that the infrastructure increases linearly with the capacity.

Name: Hard coal, burned in power plant
Description: The dataset describes the operation of an average hard coal power plant in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of some of the main characteristics (efficiency and capacity of the plant, capacity factor) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, mercury, and CO2) a bottom-up approach has been used, based upon the complete set of these factors for every US hard coal power stations in 2004. The limited number of combined heat and power plants has not been included in the analysis. All other emission data are based on US EPA (1998) and US DOE (1998) reports. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The amounts of retained SOx (due to use of FGD) and retained NOx (due to use of SCR) have been calculated as the difference between uncontrolled average US SOx and NOx emissions in year 1998 and actual region specific SOx and NOx emissions in year 2004 assuming that the characteristics of the coals have not changed in the meanwhile. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. The share of the recycled ash is the average US. For the disposal of the remaining ash, the German disposal dataset has been used, roughly representing average European environmental impacts due to hard coal ash disposal.; UUID: 7a47c38e-e80c-3505-aba2-a743a5d0c632 includedProcesses:Energy conversion for electricity production. Use of fuel oil for startup is accounted for. Particle removal is included in this module. DeSOx and DeNOx are described in different modules. The relevant SOx and NOx retention amounts have been estimated for this region with a top-down approach. SOx and NOx emissions are those finally released to air. It is assumed that 25% of the plants are river cooled, 75% use cooling towers (guestimate: same share as for European hard coal power plants). The water treatment is described in separate modules. Material requirements of cooling water, chemicals, etc, as well as wastes produced during operation are assumed to be the same as for European hard coal power plants. The amount of recycled ash is the US average. The disposal of non-recycled ashes is modelled using the German disposal dataset as approximation (it roughly exhibits average environmental impacts among the other country-specific European datasets for ash disposal). The hard coal fuel use per MJin is region specific, depending on the heating value of the consumed coal. Transport means and average distances for supply of hard coal to the modelled power plant are US averages. Power plant infrastructure is included by a mix of 100 MW and 500 MW units, whose share reproduces the average power plant capacity in this region with the simplifying assumption that the infrastructure increases linearly with the capacity.

Name: Hard coal, burned in power plant
Description: The module describes the operation of an average plant in the region. The plant is used for middle load with 4000 hours of operation at full capacity per year. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of main characteristics (LHV, sulphur and ash content of coal, efficiency of the plant) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, particles, mercury) a bottom-up approach has been used and supplemented by typical emission factors in cases of data gaps (based on EEA/EPA). CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions have been derived from fuel types (from IEA data) and IPCC emission factors. Airborne emission data has been updated for 2019, whereas other inputs and outputs come from the original dataset. The dataset consists on the collection of information about single plants. Base data on all major power plants in 2019 have been integrated, to the extent possible. The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Emissions of trace substances (except for mercury) were derived from emission factors in the literature (EEA/EPA). The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Name: Hard coal, burned in power plant
Description: The dataset describes the operation of an average hard coal power plant in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of some of the main characteristics (efficiency and capacity of the plant, capacity factor) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, mercury, and CO2) a bottom-up approach has been used, based upon the complete set of these factors for every US hard coal power stations in 2004. The limited number of combined heat and power plants has not been included in the analysis. All other emission data are based on US EPA (1998) and US DOE (1998) reports. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The amounts of retained SOx (due to use of FGD) and retained NOx (due to use of SCR) have been calculated as the difference between uncontrolled average US SOx and NOx emissions in year 1998 and actual region specific SOx and NOx emissions in year 2004 assuming that the characteristics of the coals have not changed in the meanwhile. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. The share of the recycled ash is the average US. For the disposal of the remaining ash, the German disposal dataset has been used, roughly representing average European environmental impacts due to hard coal ash disposal.; UUID: 487a3344-756a-35be-8dc3-c7b463274d52 includedProcesses:Energy conversion for electricity production. Use of fuel oil for startup is accounted for. Particle removal is included in this module. DeSOx and DeNOx are described in different modules. The relevant SOx and NOx retention amounts have been estimated for this region with a top-down approach. SOx and NOx emissions are those finally released to air. It is assumed that 25% of the plants are river cooled, 75% use cooling towers (guestimate: same share as for European hard coal power plants). The water treatment is described in separate modules. Material requirements of cooling water, chemicals, etc, as well as wastes produced during operation are assumed to be the same as for European hard coal power plants. The amount of recycled ash is the US average. The disposal of non-recycled ashes is modelled using the German disposal dataset as approximation (it roughly exhibits average environmental impacts among the other country-specific European datasets for ash disposal). The hard coal fuel use per MJin is region specific, depending on the heating value of the consumed coal. Transport means and average distances for supply of hard coal to the modelled power plant are US averages. Power plant infrastructure is included by a mix of 100 MW and 500 MW units, whose share reproduces the average power plant capacity in this region with the simplifying assumption that the infrastructure increases linearly with the capacity.

Name: Hard coal, burned in power plant
Description: The dataset describes the operation of an average hard coal power plant in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of some of the main characteristics (efficiency and capacity of the plant, capacity factor) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, mercury, and CO2) a bottom-up approach has been used, based upon the complete set of these factors for every US hard coal power stations in 2004. The limited number of combined heat and power plants has not been included in the analysis. All other emission data are based on US EPA (1998) and US DOE (1998) reports. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The amounts of retained SOx (due to use of FGD) and retained NOx (due to use of SCR) have been calculated as the difference between uncontrolled average US SOx and NOx emissions in year 1998 and actual region specific SOx and NOx emissions in year 2004 assuming that the characteristics of the coals have not changed in the meanwhile. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. The share of the recycled ash is the average US. For the disposal of the remaining ash, the German disposal dataset has been used, roughly representing average European environmental impacts due to hard coal ash disposal.; UUID: 2306a129-0704-352e-9255-dbf563b84250 includedProcesses:Energy conversion for electricity production. Use of fuel oil for startup is accounted for. Particle removal is included in this module. DeSOx and DeNOx are described in different modules. The relevant SOx and NOx retention amounts have been estimated for this region with a top-down approach. SOx and NOx emissions are those finally released to air. It is assumed that 25% of the plants are river cooled, 75% use cooling towers (guestimate: same share as for European hard coal power plants). The water treatment is described in separate modules. Material requirements of cooling water, chemicals, etc, as well as wastes produced during operation are assumed to be the same as for European hard coal power plants. The amount of recycled ash is the US average. The disposal of non-recycled ashes is modelled using the German disposal dataset as approximation (it roughly exhibits average environmental impacts among the other country-specific European datasets for ash disposal). The hard coal fuel use per MJin is region specific, depending on the heating value of the consumed coal. Transport means and average distances for supply of hard coal to the modelled power plant are US averages. Power plant infrastructure is included by a mix of 100 MW and 500 MW units, whose share reproduces the average power plant capacity in this region with the simplifying assumption that the infrastructure increases linearly with the capacity.

Description:
Translated name: Erdgas, in Kraftwerk oder Heizkraftwerk
Included processes: The module includes fuel input from the natural gas network, infrastructure, emissions to air, and substances needed for operation.

The module describes the operation of an average plant in the region. The plant is used for middle load with 4000 hours of operation at full capacity per year. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of main characteristics and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, particles) a bottom-up approach has been used and supplemented by typical emission factors in cases of data gaps (based on EEA/EPA). CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions have been derived from fuel type and IPCC emission factors. Airborne emission data has been updated for 2021, whereas other inputs and outputs come from the original dataset. The dataset consists on the collection of information about single plants. Base data on all major power plants and heat plants in 2021 have been integrated, to the extent possible. The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Emissions of trace substances were derived from emission factors in the literature (EEA/EPA).

Name: Hard coal, burned in power plant
Description: The dataset describes the operation of an average hard coal power plant in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of some of the main characteristics (efficiency and capacity of the plant, capacity factor) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, mercury, and CO2) a bottom-up approach has been used, based upon the complete set of these factors for every US hard coal power stations in 2004. The limited number of combined heat and power plants has not been included in the analysis. All other emission data are based on US EPA (1998) and US DOE (1998) reports. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The amounts of retained SOx (due to use of FGD) and retained NOx (due to use of SCR) have been calculated as the difference between uncontrolled average US SOx and NOx emissions in year 1998 and actual region specific SOx and NOx emissions in year 2004 assuming that the characteristics of the coals have not changed in the meanwhile. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. The share of the recycled ash is the average US. For the disposal of the remaining ash, the German disposal dataset has been used, roughly representing average European environmental impacts due to hard coal ash disposal.; UUID: af196159-e1c7-3533-ad78-bb6ad8d27f25 includedProcesses:Energy conversion for electricity production. Use of fuel oil for startup is accounted for. Particle removal is included in this module. DeSOx and DeNOx are described in different modules. The relevant SOx and NOx retention amounts have been estimated for this region with a top-down approach. SOx and NOx emissions are those finally released to air. It is assumed that 25% of the plants are river cooled, 75% use cooling towers (guestimate: same share as for European hard coal power plants). The water treatment is described in separate modules. Material requirements of cooling water, chemicals, etc, as well as wastes produced during operation are assumed to be the same as for European hard coal power plants. The amount of recycled ash is the US average. The disposal of non-recycled ashes is modelled using the German disposal dataset as approximation (it roughly exhibits average environmental impacts among the other country-specific European datasets for ash disposal). The hard coal fuel use per MJin is region specific, depending on the heating value of the consumed coal. Transport means and average distances for supply of hard coal to the modelled power plant are US averages. Power plant infrastructure is included by a mix of 100 MW and 500 MW units, whose share reproduces the average power plant capacity in this region with the simplifying assumption that the infrastructure increases linearly with the capacity.

Name: Natural gas, burned in power plant or heat plant
Description:
Translated name: Erdgas, in Kraftwerk oder Heizkraftwerk
Included processes: The module includes fuel input from the natural gas network, infrastructure, emissions to air, and substances needed for operation.

The module describes the operation of an average plant in the region. The plant is used for middle load with 4000 hours of operation at full capacity per year. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of main characteristics and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, particles) a bottom-up approach has been used and supplemented by typical emission factors in cases of data gaps (based on EEA/EPA). CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions have been derived from fuel type and IPCC emission factors. Airborne emission data has been updated for 2021, whereas other inputs and outputs come from the original dataset. The dataset consists on the collection of information about single plants. Base data on all major power plants and heat plants in 2021 have been integrated, to the extent possible. The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Emissions of trace substances were derived from emission factors in the literature (EEA/EPA).

Description:

Included processes: The module includes fuel input from the natural gas network, infrastructure, emissions to air, and substances needed for operation.

The module describes the operation of an average plant in the region. The plant is used for middle load with 4000 hours of operation at full capacity per year. The plant is assumed to operate 150000 hours during its lifetime. For the assessment of main characteristics and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, particles) a bottom-up approach has been used and supplemented by typical emission factors in cases of data gaps (based on EEA/EPA). CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions have been derived from fuel type and IPCC emission factors. Airborne emission data has been updated for 2021, whereas other inputs and outputs come from the original dataset. The dataset consists on the collection of information about single plants. Base data on all major power plants and heat plants in 2021 have been integrated, to the extent possible. The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Emissions of trace substances were derived from emission factors in the literature (EEA/EPA).

Name: Electricity, nuclear, at power plant pressure water reactor
Description: The dataset has been developed on the basis of the operation of the average US PWR with average burnup of 37.5 MWd-th/kg heavy metal (reload 2006) assumed representative for the lifetime of the modelled plant. The average burnup corresponds to an average enrichment of 3.8% U235 for fuel elements, all using fresh uranium because reprocessing is not permitted in the USA. The utilisation factor for the infrastructure is the inverse of the total net electricity delivered in 40 years lifetime, calculated assuming an average Load Factor = 85% (2003-2006 LF was 90.9% but lifetime LF up to September 2006 was 77.8%). Material requirements have been extrapolated from the Swiss PWR by the ratio of the capacity factors. The transport requirements for materials (e.g. chemicals) are calculated using ecoinvent standard distances for Europe. Radioactive emission species to air and water are taken from US data of all individual PWR units and represent the average in the time period 2000-2005. Water use (fresh from sea and decarbonized) for cooling is included. For the assessment of main characteristics (LHV, sulphur and ash content of coal, efficiency of the plant) and criteria emissions (SOx, NOx, particles, mercury) a bottom-up approach has been used and supplemented by typical emission factors in cases of data gaps (based on EEA/EPA). CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions have been derived from fuel types (from IEA data) and IPCC emission factors. Airborne emission data has been updated for 2019, whereas other inputs and outputs come from the original dataset. The dataset consists on the collection of information about single plants. Base data on all major power plants in 2019 have been integrated, to the extent possible. The size distribution of particles has been derived from non-linear calculations based on typical ratios for different total emission amounts based on CEPMEIP. Emissions of trace substances (except for mercury) were derived from emission factors in the literature (EEA/EPA). The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air. The share of the recycled ash is country-specific. For the disposal of the remaining ash, typical country-specific compositions are taken into account in appropriate disposal modules. Description: The dataset describes the electricity production at an average hard coal power plant at busbar in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The limited number of combined heat and power plants has not been included in the analysis. All other emission data are based on US EPA (1998) and US DOE (1998) reports. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The amounts of retained SOx (due to use of FGD) and retained NOx (due to use of SCR) have been calculated as the difference between uncontrolled average US SOx and NOx emissions in year 1998 and actual region specific SOx and NOx emissions in year 2004 assuming that the characteristics of the coals have not changed in the meanwhile. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. Description: The dataset describes the electricity production at an average hard coal power plant at busbar in this region of the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC), modelled separately from the other regions. The size distribution of particles has been derived from German data, assumed as well representative for European hard coal power plants. The waste heat releases to air and water have been allocated on the basis of the assumed share of cooling tower vs. river cooled power plants and assumptions on the direct losses to air, along with the corresponding European datasets. All coalbed methane released from the seam is accounted for as natural gas resource. Name: Biochar, from spruce wood pyrolysis
Description:
This dataset represents the production of 1 kilogram of biochar through slow pyrolysis. Biochar yield of 27.9% (of the dry feedstock), bio-oil (55%) and gas (17%). Annual plant capacity: 10'000 t fresh feedstock = 6000 t dry feedstock. The energy needed for pyrolysis, excluding drying (273.59 GJ electricity and 1316.65 GJ of thermal energy required to produce 1673.33 t biochar), was back-calculated from data in Tisserant, A., Morales, M., Cavalett, O., O'Toole, A., Weldon, S., Rasse, D. P., & Cherubini, F. (2022). Life-cycle assessment to unravel co-benefits and trade-offs of large-scale biochar deployment in Norwegian agriculture. Resources, Conservation and Recycling, 179, 106030. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2021.106030, using their supplementary information. Using the cutoff approach for the byproducts.

The yield of biochar is calculated on a dry ash-free basis (DAF) using the following formula: 0.126+0.273*(FSlignin/100)+0.539*EXP(-0.004*Tp, C) where:
- FS lignin represents the Lignin content of the feedstock, which is expressed as a percentage.
- Tp, C is pyrolysis temperature (Â°C)
- exp(âˆ’0.004â‹…T p, C ) represents an exponential decay factor (biochar yield decreases with increasing pyrolysis temperature)

The carbon content of biochar is calculated as a fraction of the dry ash-free biochar using the following formula: 0.93âˆ’0.92â‹…exp(âˆ’0.0042â‹…T p, C) where Tp, C is pyrolysis temperature (Â°C) and exp(âˆ’0.0042â‹…Tp, C): Exponential decay (carbon content stabilizes at higher temperatures)

The oxygen content of biochar is calculated as a fraction of the dry ash-free biochar using the following formula: âˆ’0.0041+0.1â‹…exp(âˆ’0.0024â‹…T p, C ). exp(âˆ’0.0024â‹…T p, C) represents an exponential decay (oxygen content decreases with increasing pyrolysis temperature).

The hydrogen content of biochar is calculated using the following formula: 0.07+0.85â‹…exp(âˆ’0.0048â‹…T p, C)

The gaseous yields such as CO, H2, CH4, C2H2 are also calculated using the respective formulas:
(CO) (0.043/(1+exp(17.2âˆ’0.03â‹…T p,K )))+(0.317/(1+exp(10.9âˆ’0.01â‹…T p,K)))
(H2) 0.0295â‹…(1âˆ’exp(âˆ’0.0035â‹…T p,K ))^62.98
(CH4) 0.0782â‹…(1âˆ’exp(âˆ’0.00338â‹…T p,K))^30.15
(C2H2) 0.036â‹…(1âˆ’exp(âˆ’0.00522â‹…T p, K ))^154.97, pyrolysis temperature in this case is expressed in Kelvin.
 A matrix is used to allocate the elemental components (C, O, H) of the feedstock into the pyrolysis products: tar, COâ‚‚, and Hâ‚‚O. The use of the matrix ensures mass conservation for each element (C, O, H) and allows the calculation of yields for tar, COâ‚‚, and Hâ‚‚O based on the initial feedstock composition. The calculations result in bio-oil yields (55% yield, DAF) with an HHV of 16.3 GJ/Mg and of the pyrolysis Gas (17% yield, DAF) with an HHV of 6.8 GJ/Mg.

Source: Hoeskuldsdottir, Gudrun. 2022. Life Cycle Assessment of Biochar to Soil Systems: A Parametric Analysis. Masterâ€™s thesis, Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ZÃ¼rich and Paul Scherrer Institute.

Name: Hard coal, at mine
Description: Update 2022 by ZHAW only updated methane emissions at mine, Remark: Average data for coal mining in the specific region have been taken from a summary study on material flows and energy uses. Data are normalized by the mass unit of produced coal, including preparation and without differentiating steam coal from the rest. In order to enable a consistent calculation of the cumulative energy demand, the extracted mass of raw coal was adjusted by a factor of 0.91, taking into account the difference in the upper heating value of raw coal of this region (17.3 MJ/kg), compared to the used worldwide average of 19.1 MJ/kg. Mine reclamation is not included in this module, because it mostly concerns the tailings, which are described in a separate module. Electricity, heating from heavy oil industrial boilers, and diesel uses are included. The use of the module "heat, at hard coal industrial furnace 1-10MW" leads to an underestimation of emissions, because the quality of coal burned at mines is usually lower than coal burned in industrial boilers elsewhere. Electricity supply is modelled with the UCTE mix, because no specific mix has been modelled. Water uses in mining and coal washing have been approximately described using the module "tap water". Particle emissions are assumed to be all greater than 10 micrometer. Radon emissions are average value worldwide. Methane emissions are region specific. Emissions to water are estimated for Western European conditions and applied to this region. They are assumed to be released to rivers. Possible emissions to groundwater have not been accounted for. All coalbed methane released from the seam is accounted for as natural gas resource. However the recovered methane, possibly used for district heating and for energetic needs of some individual mines, has not been described as an energy byproduct. The unaccounted energy is nevertheless negligible compared to the energy content of the product coal (maximum of two percent for underground mining).; NA; UUID: 3a0025dc-a2a7-4550-835c-b29f19c04548 includedProcesses:Included processes: The module represents average operational conditions in the relevant geographical region. It quantifies the directly affected area and occupation during operation of the mine. Electricity, heat, and diesel requirements for mining operation are included. Pumped groundwater, explosives, emissions to air and water, and solid waste complete the module. Not included is the methane recovered.

Name: Hard coal, at mine
Description: Update 2022 by ZHAW only updated methane emissions at mine, Remark: Average data for coal mining in the specific region have been taken from a summary study on material flows and energy uses. Data are normalized by the mass unit of produced coal, including preparation and without differentiating steam coal from the rest. In order to enable a consistent calculation of the cumulative energy demand, the extracted mass of raw coal was adjusted by a factor of 1.05, taking into account the difference in the upper heating value of raw coal of this region (20.1 MJ/kg), compared to the used worldwide average of 19.1 MJ/kg. Mine reclamation is not included in this module, because it mostly concerns the tailings, which are described in a separate module. Electricity, heating from heavy oil industrial boilers, and diesel uses are included. The use of the module "heat, at hard coal industrial furnace 1-10MW" leads to an underestimation of emissions, because the quality of coal burned at mines is usually lower than coal burned in industrial boilers elsewhere. Electricity supply is modelled with the UCTE mix, because no specific mix has been modelled. Water uses in mining and coal washing have been approximately described using the module "tap water". Particle emissions are assumed to be all greater than 10 micrometer. Radon emissions are average value worldwide. Methane emissions are region specific. Emissions to water are estimated for Western European conditions and applied to this region. They are assumed to be released to rivers. Possible emissions to groundwater have not been accounted for. All coalbed methane released from the seam is accounted for as natural gas resource.; NA; UUID: 3e264d8a-b0b3-46b5-aa7b-2183ce36086c includedProcesses:Included processes: The module represents average operational conditions in the relevant geographical region. It quantifies the directly affected area and occupation during operation of the mine. Electricity, heat, and diesel requirements for mining operation are included. Pumped groundwater, explosives, emissions to air and water, and solid waste complete the module.

Name: Carbon dioxide, captured from atmosphere, with adsorbent-based direct air capture system, operated with HP, 100kt CO2
Description:
Direct Air Capture (DAC) of CO2 through temperature-vacuum swing adsorption. This DAC process uses adsorbents to capture CO2 from the air and separates it through vacuum and low-temperature heating. Climeworks provides data from its commercial DAC plants, which consist of multiple CO2 collectors and heat exchangers, capturing and releasing CO2 in cyclic operations. The solid sorbent used here is Amine on Silica. It can be regenerated at low temperatures (80-120C). For the sorbent system, the LCI data are collected from the work of Deutz and Bardow based on the Climeworks system. The LCI data represent a plant with an annual capacity of 100 kt CO2/year and a lifetime of 20 years. 

Source: Deutz, S., Bardow, A. Life-cycle assessment of an industrial direct air capture process based on temperature-vacuum swing adsorption. Nat Energy 6, (2021). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-00771-9. Assumes "future" electricity consumption of 0.5 kWh/kg CO2 captured as per Deutz and Bardow, 2021. Current electricity consumption is closer to 0.7 kWh/kg CO2 captured. Future heat demand is 5.4 MJ/kg CO2 captured, as per Deutz and Bardow, 2021. The current demand is closer to 11.9. Future MEA consumption is 3 kg/t CO2 captured. Current consumption is closer to 7 kg/t CO2 captured, as per Deutz and Bardow, 2021.

Name: Carbon dioxide, captured at cement production plant, for subsequent reuse
Description:
Capture of CO2 from a cement plant for subsequent reuse. It is a facility integrated in a synthetic fuel production chain, so a certain amount of the needed steam heat (used to regenerate the sorbent) can come from excess heat generated by the synfuel conversion process, the rest being complemented by a dedicated source. In Meunier et al. 2020, 26% comes from excess heat generated by the methanol production process. To be changed according to needs. Also, there is no need for water, as it is provided by the methanol production process as well. CO2 chemical absorption-regeneration process using amines as scrubbing solvent. The amine solution used for this absorption was an aqueous solution of monoethanolamine (MEA) in a mass concentration of 30 wt.%, widely studied and considered as a benchmark for industrial CO2 capture applications. The CO2 is pre-compressed at 2 bar before storage. 11% of the CO2 is released back into the atmosphere (because the CO2 absoprtion rate is only 90%). The MEA makeup has been considered to 1 kg MEA per ton captured CO2 to compensate the losses due to the thermal degradation of the amine only, as the evaporation of the amine in the absorber is prevented by a flash tank. The rate of fossil vs. biogenic CO2 received from the cement plant need to be reflected in this dataset in two places: at the leakage level, but also at the storage level. At the storage level, we only indicate biogenic CO2. By default, we asusme 6% of the CO2 emissions are biogenic. Source: Alternative production of methanol from industrial CO2. Meunier et al. 2020. Renewable Energy 146, pp. 1192-1203

Name: Gold, primary, at refinery
Carbon dioxide, captured at cement production plant, with heat recovery, for subsequent reuse
Description:
Capture of CO2 from a cement plant for subsequent reuse. It is a facility integrated in a synthetic fuel production chain, so a certain amount of the needed steam heat (used to regenerate the sorbent) can come from excess heat generated by the synfuel conversion process, the rest being complemented by a dedicated source. In Meunier et al. 2020, 26% comes from excess heat generated by the methanol production process. To be changed according to needs. Also, there is no need for water, as it is provided by the methanol production process as well. CO2 chemical absorption-regeneration process using amines as scrubbing solvent. The amine solution used for this absorption was an aqueous solution of monoethanolamine (MEA) in a mass concentration of 30 wt.%, widely studied and considered as a benchmark for industrial CO2 capture applications. The CO2 is pre-compressed at 2 bar before storage. 11% of the CO2 is released back into the atmosphere (because the CO2 absoprtion rate is only 90%). The MEA makeup has been considered to 1 kg MEA per ton captured CO2 to compensate the losses due to the thermal degradation of the amine only, as the evaporation of the amine in the absorber is prevented by a flash tank. The rate of fossil vs. biogenic CO2 received from the cement plant need to be reflected in this dataset in two places: at the leakage level, but also at the storage level. At the storage level, we only indicate biogenic CO2. By default, we asusme 6% of the CO2 emissions are biogenic. Here, heat recovery from the cement plant's flue. gases is considered to the extent of 30% of the heat requirement by the capture plant (2.5 GJ/t CO2 captured, instead of 3.66). Source: Alternative production of methanol from industrial CO2. Meunier et al. 2020. Renewable Energy 146, pp. 1192-1203

Name: Uranium, enriched 4.0%, at USEC enrichment plant
Description: This module does not use a full, consistent set of data specific for the only operational USEC plant in Paducah, for there is no available literature source on that. However the data on the US "model diffusion plants" available in the literature and used herewith were most likely developed on the basis of the existing US facilities. The electricity consumption per unit of SWU of 2600 kWh/SWU is an average value from the literature. Extrapolating direct information from the plant operators, the electricity is assumed to be supplied almost entirely by the Tennessee Valley Authority (base load). The used mix is made of nearly 69% hard coal, about 26% nuclear, and about 5% run-of-river hydropower. Hence, the indirect environmental burdens imported through the high electricity uses are fully represented. Only little information was available for emission species to air and water from the US model diffusion plants, but an average emission of CFC-114 estimated from 2002 data is accounted for. The factor for the infrastructure requirement is calculated using an average capacity of two USEC plants of 9600 t SWU for assumed 50 years operation.; UUID: 9aa45e8f-a045-36f6-ad56-a97f3b6ca878 includedProcesses:The module includes: input of UF6; electricity and light fuel oil used for operation; water use, lubricant oil, and wastewater treatment; transport requirements of operation materials, industrial wastes, and contaminated waste from decommissioning (25% of the reinforced concrete and the great part of metals according to the reference). Radioactive and non-radioactive emissions to air and to water from the operation are also included. The infrastructure requirements are accounted for, though construction and operation data partially refer to different plants rather than to one single unit.

Name: Hard coal, at mine
Description: Update 2022 by ZHAW only updated methane emissions at mine, Remark: Average data for coal mining in the specific region have been taken from a summary study on material flows and energy uses. Data are normalized by the mass unit of produced coal, including preparation and without differentiating steam coal from the rest. Due to a lack of data, the upper heating value of raw coal of this region had to be estimated as the used worldwide average of 19.1 MJ/kg n order to enable a consistent calculation of the cumulative energy demand. Mine reclamation is not included in this module, because it mostly concerns the tailings, which are described in a separate module. Electricity, heating from heavy oil industrial boilers, and diesel uses are included. The use of the module "heat, at hard coal industrial furnace 1-10MW" leads to an underestimation of emissions, because the quality of coal burned at mines is usually lower than coal burned in industrial boilers elsewhere. Electricity supply is modelled with the UCTE mix, because no specific mix has been modelled. Water uses in mining and coal washing have been approximately described using the module "tap water". Particle emissions are assumed to be all greater than 10 micrometer. Radon emissions are average value worldwide. Methane emissions are region specific. Emissions to water are estimated for Western European conditions and applied to this region. They are assumed to be released to rivers. Possible emissions to groundwater have not been accounted for. All coalbed methane released from the seam is accounted for as natural gas resource. However the recovered methane, possibly used for district heating and for energetic needs of some individual mines, has not been described as an energy byproduct. The unaccounted energy is nevertheless negligible compared to the energy content of the product coal (maximum of two percent for underground mining).; NA; UUID: 9ae6bea7-4875-4644-9b87-4c4fb1ee48eb includedProcesses:Included processes: The module represents average operational conditions in the relevant geographical region. It quantifies the directly affected area and occupation during operation of the mine. Electricity, heat, and diesel requirements for mining operation are included. Pumped groundwater, explosives, emissions to air and water, and solid waste complete the module. Not included is the methane recovered.

Name: Hard coal coke, at plant
Description: The multioutput-prozess "hard coal, in coke plant" delivers the coproducts "coke oven gas, at plant", "tar, at coke plant", and "benzene, at coke plant". 79.8% of the total energy and material input as well as emission from the coke plant are allocated to coke production, 15% to coke oven gas production, 4.1% to tar production, and 1.1% to benzene production. This allocation has been performed considering the energy content of the coke compared to all other byproducts. Due to lack of information, the allocation factors are the same as for Germany. Hypothesizing that coke production worldwide is mostly based on the byproduct process, this is described here. Emission data are maximum for US plants. Energy and material consumption as well as water emission and solid waste are taken from the DE module.  The assumed uncertainty factors should somewhat frame the incomplete information about coke making outside Europe and USA. This module shall be considered only as a first approximation for the purpose to serve metal manufacturing processes within ecoinvent. In some countries coke making might exhibit worse environmental performance. Hence, when country-specific LCA studies will need to address coke making directly or indirectly, a specific assessment of local conditions should be pursued.; UUID: 27ed6f5d-a100-3bb5-b6b9-a4047b7459af includedProcesses:The reference process has been assumed to be the byproduct coke production, used in almost all US coke plants in 1998. The coke making has been considered as a black box. The energy necessary for the process is assumed to be provided by part of the input coal and by some electricity. The module includes chemicals used for operation and the associated transport requirements. The transport of coal are considered to be negligible, because the plant is assumed to be mine-mouth. The module also includes the total emissions to air and water from the entire plant. Coke oven gas, tar, and benzene are byproducts of coking.

Name: Hydrogen production, gaseous, 100 bar, from pyrolysis of liquefied natural gas
Description:
1 kg H2 produced by pyrolyzing methane from Algerian liquefied natural gas. Pyrolysis processes decompose hydrocarbons into solid carbon and hydrogen at high temperatures (thermally or biologicalally). As no oxygen is present, no carbon oxides are formed, potentially eliminating the need for secondary processing steps such as the WGSR. The higher H2 concentration of the product gas stream also has considerable potential for minimising downstream clean-up processes. From a carbon-storage perspective, pyrolysis processes offer the advantage of storing a solid C-product as opposed to gaseous CO2. There is no alloc. of the process burden between the co-production of hydrogen and black carbon: the entirety of the burden is attributed to hydrogen production. Source: Amjad Al-Qahtani, Brett Parkinson, Klaus Hellgardt, Nilay Shah, Gonzalo Guillen-Gosalbez, Uncovering the true cost of hydrogen production routes using life cycle monetisation, Applied Energy, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1/j.apenergy0.20.12. The energy required is from DOI:10.1/ceat0.2. For pyrolysis, it can be provided both electrically and by burning some of the natural gas or pyrolysis products. For the comparison of technologies, electrical resistance heating is assumed, as use of this type of heating is deemed to be most practicable. The power requirement of 7.23 MWhel/ton H2 is based on thermodynamic calculations. These take into account both the energy losses during heat recovery and the compression power of 2 MWhel/ton H2, to compress pyrolysis hydrogen from 2 bar to 100 bar with three interim cooling stages. Inventories consolidated with numbers for infrastructures from Appendix A1 from Postels et al., 2016 https://doi.org/10.1/j.ijhydene0.20.090.17. Missing input of quartz for reactor, as unavailable in ecoinvent.

Name: Carbon dioxide, captured at municipal solid waste incineration plant, for subsequent reuse
Description:
The MEA technology considered for this study is modelled after Tang and You, 2018, Reiter and Lindorfer, 2015. After flue gas condensation, the cooled flue gas is fed into a reactor containing a 30% MEA solution, which absorbs around 85â€“90% of the CO2, typically at 25 Â°Câ€“50 Â°C at 1 bar. The process is exothermic. The CO2-rich solution is heated afterwards to 100â€“140 Â°C, and in a stripper at 1â€“2 bars the CO2 desorbs from the MEA and leaves saturated with water vapour. The water is then condensed from the CO2 stream, and the CO2 is compressed to around 150 bar for transporting in pipes or a lower pressure for local tank storage and shipment by truck. The recovered MEA is reused in the plant (Pour et al., 2018). About 4 kg of MEA is used per tonne of CO2, due to degradation (releasing around 0.1 kg NH3 per tonne CO2 captured), the formation of heat-stable salts and losses as vapour and aerosols during stripping (the latter is around 0.01 kg per tonne of CO2 captured). NaOH is added in the stripping step at an amount of 0.1 kg per tonne CO2 captured. Around 4 kg of solid waste is generated per tonne of CO2 captured; this waste is disregarded. The MEA CC process also reduces the content of other pollutants in the flue gas, the extent of which depends on whether flue gas condensation is already in place or is introduced as part of the CO2 capture system. SOx, HCl, particulate matter and heavy metals are reduced to very low levels by flue gas condensation and subsequent CC. The level of NH3 increases in the flue gas after CC because of degradation of MEA. This is not included here. Source: Valentina Bisinella, Tore Hulgaard, Christian Riber, Anders Damgaard, Thomas H. Christensen, Environmental assessment of carbon capture and storage (CCS) as a post-treatment technology in waste incineration, Waste Management, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1/j.wasman0.20.040.05.

Name: Integrated circuit, IC, memory type, at plant
Description: This dataset can be applied to describe the entire production of a memory type integrated circuit. The required the infrastructure, and the ship, train and road transport are also inventoried. Calculated for 1 kg of packaged memory IC.

Name: Treatment of heat pump 10 kW production for air source heat pump system
Description:
10.55 kW GSHP system operating in New Jersey, US. The system boundary spans the entire lifetime of a GSHP system, including: borehole drilling and heat exchanger installation, heat pump production and installation, system operation and maintenance, and end-of-life. The overall efficiency of the system was assumed to have a heating coefficient of performance (COPheating) of 3.5. The system life is assumed to be 25 years. For the ground loop installation, we assume two boreholes each drilled at a depth of 80 m to represent a vertical closed-loop system. Source: Meghann Smith, Anthony Bevacqua, Sheryl Tembe, Pankaj Lal. Life cycle analysis (LCA) of residential ground source heat pump systems: A comparative analysis of energy efficiency in New Jersey, Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments, Volume 47, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.seta.2021.101364.

Name: Hard coal, at mine
Description: Update 2022 by ZHAW only updated methane emissions at mine, Remark: Average data for coal mining in the specific region have been taken from a summary study on material flows and energy uses. Data are normalized by the mass unit of produced coal, including preparation and without differentiating steam coal from the rest. In order to enable a consistent calculation of the cumulative energy demand, the extracted mass of raw coal was adjusted by a factor of 0.84, taking into account the difference in the upper heating value of raw coal of this region (16.1 MJ/kg), compared to the used worldwide average of 19.1 MJ/kg. Mine reclamation is not included in this module, because it mostly concerns the tailings, which are described in a separate module. Electricity, heating from heavy oil industrial boilers, and diesel uses are included. The use of the module "heat, at hard coal industrial furnace 1-10MW" leads to an underestimation of emissions, because the quality of coal burned at mines is usually lower than coal burned in industrial boilers elsewhere.  Electricity supply is modelled with the UCTE mix, because no specific mix has been modelled. Water uses in mining and coal washing have been approximately described using the module "tap water". Particle emissions are assumed to be all greater than 10 micrometer. Radon emissions are average value worldwide. Methane emissions are region specific. Emissions to water are estimated for Western European conditions and applied to this region. They are assumed to be released to rivers. Possible emissions to groundwater have not been accounted for. All coalbed methane released from the seam is accounted for as natural gas resource. However the recovered methane, possibly used for district heating and for energetic needs of some individual mines, has not been described as an energy byproduct. The unaccounted energy is nevertheless negligible compared to the energy content of the product coal (maximum of two percent for underground mining).; NA; UUID: 2148e2ca-7400-4cc6-a216-8d5dd07d8e59 includedProcesses:Included processes: The module represents average operational conditions in the relevant geographical region. It quantifies the directly affected area and occupation during operation of the mine. Electricity, heat, and diesel requirements for mining operation are included. Pumped groundwater, explosives, emissions to air and water, and solid waste complete the module. Not included is the methane recovered.

Name: xx Benzene, at coke plant
Description: The multioutput-prozess "hard coal, in coke plant" delivers the coproducts "coke oven gas, at plant", "tar, at coke plant", and "benzene, at coke plant". 79.8% of the total energy and material input as well as emission from the coke plant are allocated to coke production, 15% to coke oven gas production, 4.1% to tar production, and 1.1% to benzene production. This allocation has been performed considering the energy content of the coke compared to all other byproducts. Due to lack of information, the allocation factors are the same as for Germany. Hypothesizing that coke production worldwide is mostly based on the byproduct process, this is described here. Emission data are maximum for US plants. Energy and material consumption as well as water emission and solid waste are taken from the DE module.  The assumed uncertainty factors should somewhat frame the incomplete information about coke making outside Europe and USA. This module shall be considered only as a first approximation for the purpose to serve metal manufacturing processes within ecoinvent. In some countries coke making might exhibit worse environmental performance. Hence, when country-specific LCA studies will need to address coke making directly or indirectly, a specific assessment of local conditions should be pursued.; UUID: 2596643c-5ab9-3328-b725-c925b39716a6 includedProcesses:The reference process has been assumed to be the byproduct coke production, used in almost all US coke plants in 1998. The coke making has been considered as a black box. The energy necessary for the process is assumed to be provided by part of the input coal and by some electricity. The module includes chemicals used for operation and the associated transport requirements. The transport of coal are considered to be negligible, because the plant is assumed to be mine-mouth. The module also includes the total emissions to air and water from the entire plant. Coke oven gas, tar, and benzene are byproducts of coking.

Name: Uranium, enriched 3.0% at TENEX enrichment plant
Description: This module uses a mix of data, some specific for the URENCO facilities taken from environmental reports, some from literature. The infrastructure requirements are accounted for, though construction and operation data partially refer to different plants rather than to one single unit.

Resources, Conservation and Recycling, 179, 106030. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2021.106030) with a conversion factor to dry ton of 0.6. The feedstock is assumed to be dried to zero moisture content to be on the safe side in accounting for the energy requirements of evaporating water at all stages. Rotary drier requirements: 0.1 GJ electricity/tonnes of water and 2.7 GJ thermal energy/tonnes of water. Electricity and heat requirements are taken from Manouchehrinejad, M., & Mani, S. (2019). Process simulation of an integrated biomass torrefaction and pelletization (iBTP) plant to produce solid biofuels. Energy Conversion and Management: X, 1, 100008. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecmx.2019.100008. Electric chipping requirements: 0.0005 GJ/ MJfsdry. The requirements for electric chipping are taken from Kuptz, D., & Hartmann, H. (2014). Throughput Rate and Energy Consumption During Wood Chip Production in Relation to Raw Material, Chipper Type and Machine Setting. https://doi.org/10.5071/22ndEUBCE2014-2CO.1.5. The distance from the collection point to the plant is assumed to be 100km.

Name: Hard coal, at mine
Description: Average data for coal mining in the specific region have been taken from a summary study on material flows and energy uses. Data are normalized by the mass unit of produced coal, including preparation and without differentiating steam coal from the rest. In order to enable a consistent calculation of the cumulative energy demand, the extracted mass of raw coal was adjusted by a factor of 0.83, taking into account the difference in the upper heating value of raw coal of this region (15.8 MJ/kg), compared to the used worldwide average of 19.1 MJ/kg. Mine reclamation is not included in this module, because it mostly concerns the tailings, which are described in a separate module. Electricity, heating from heavy oil industrial boilers, and diesel uses are included. The use of the module "heat, at hard coal industrial furnace 1-10MW" leads to an underestimation of emissions, because the quality of coal burned at mines is usually lower than coal burned in industrial boilers elsewhere. Electricity supply is modelled with the UCTE mix, because no specific mix has been modelled. Water uses in mining and coal washing have been approximately described using the module "tap water". Particle emissions are assumed to be all greater than 10 micrometer. Radon emissions are average value worldwide. Methane emissions are region specific. Emissions to water are estimated for Western European conditions. They are assumed to be released to rivers. Possible emissions to groundwater have not been accounted for. All coalbed methane released from the seam is accounted for as natural gas resource. However the recovered methane, possibly used for district heating and for energetic needs of some individual mines, has not been described as an energy byproduct. The unaccounted energy is nevertheless negligible compared to the energy content of the product coal (maximum of two percent for underground mining).; UUID: a317c66b-9fee-3209-b6e0-084333ce503d includedProcesses:The module represents average operational conditions in the relevant geographical region. Name: Uranium, enriched 3.0%, at USEC enrichment plant
Description: This module does not use a full, consistent set of data specific for the only operational USEC plant in Paducah, for there is no available literature source on that. Due to extremely limited information on Chinese plants, of somewhat outdated Russian technology, all requirements and emissions are arbitrarily assumed the double of the URENCO module, along the dataset for TENEX. However, the CNNC facility is assumed to consume 170 kWh/SWU (after one reference), which should include all energy uses (electric + thermal, as electric equivalent). The factor for the infrastructure requirement is calculated with annual throughput of 1500 t SWU for 30 years operation. Transport requirements recalculated either using ecoinvent standard distances for Europe (e.g. for chemicals) or given average distances by train from Chinese 2004 statistivcs or own assumptions. This dataset has been developed with the goal to serve a preliminary estimation of the Chinese nuclear chain for the Chinese electricity mix. Hence, it cannot be used for comparisons of centrifuge enrichment among countrie; UUID: bc1633aa-18f4-32b2-acb2-e4f4f0df0bd3 includedProcesses:The module is an extrapolation of the corresponding one for URENCO. The module includes: input of UF6; electricity, diesel, and natural gas used for operation; also taken into account is the material for replacement of centrifuge; water use, lubricant oil, and wastewater treatment; concrete assumed to be used for conditioning of contaminated scrap from decommissioning; transport requirements of operation materials, industrial wastes, and contaminated waste from decommissioning (25% of the reinforced concrete and the great part of metals according to the reference). Radioactive and non-radioactive emissions to air and to water from the operation are also included. The infrastructure requirements are accounted for, though construction and operation data partially refer to different plants rather than to one single unit.

Name: Uranium, enriched 4.0%, at TENEX enrichment plant
Description: This module uses a mix of data, some specific for the URENCO facilities taken from environmental reports, some from literature. Due to lack of information on Russian plants, all requirements and emissions are arbitrarily assumed the double of the URENCO module. Only (but still approximate) information available for TENEX facility is the electricity consumption by machines of two recent generations. A mix of generations has been assumed here, assuming conservatively a high value for auxiliary electricity (i.e., not directly used for spinning the centrifuges). The Russian electricity mix is used, which has been has been approximated using existing ecoinvent v2.0 electricity datasets for Europe. The factor for the infrastructure requirement is calculated with annual throughput of 1500 t SWU for 30 years operation (the Russian facilities are larger but this should not affect much the figures normalized by the total production).; UUID: c97573eb-d993-3743-9eae-d05ee8832604 includedProcesses:The module is an extrapolation of the corresponding one for URENCO. The module includes: input of UF6; electricity, diesel, and natural gas used for operation; also taken into account is the material for replacement of centrifuge; water use, lubricant oil, and wastewater treatment; concrete assumed to be used for conditioning of contaminated scrap from decommissioning; transport requirements of operation materials, industrial wastes, and contaminated waste from decommissioning (25% of the reinforced concrete and the great part of metals according to the reference). Radioactive and non-radioactive emissions to air and to water from the operation are also included. The infrastructure requirements are accounted for, though construction and operation data partially refer to different plants rather than to one single unit.

Name: Tar, at coke plant
Description: The multioutput-prozess "hard coal, in coke plant" delivers the coproducts "coke oven gas, at plant", "tar, at coke plant", and "benzene, at coke plant". 79.8% of the total energy and material input as well as emission from the coke plant are allocated to coke production, 15% to coke oven gas production, 4.1% to tar production, and 1.1% to benzene production. This allocation has been performed considering the energy content of the coke compared to all other byproducts. Due to lack of information, the allocation factors are the same as for Germany. Hypothesizing that coke production worldwide is mostly based on the byproduct process, this is described here. Emission data are maximum for US plants. Energy and material consumption as well as water emission and solid waste are taken from the DE module.  The assumed uncertainty factors should somewhat frame the incomplete information about coke making outside Europe and USA. This module shall be considered only as a first approximation for the purpose to serve metal manufacturing processes within ecoinvent. In some countries coke making might exhibit worse environmental performance. Hence, when country-specific LCA studies will need to address coke making directly or indirectly, a specific assessment of local conditions should be pursued.; UUID: c794607a-7879-3421-bd69-9f3236ca5aa9 includedProcesses:The reference process has been assumed to be the byproduct coke production, used in almost all US coke plants in 1998. The coke making has been considered as a black box. The energy necessary for the process is assumed to be provided by part of the input coal and by some electricity. The module includes chemicals used for operation and the associated transport requirements. The transport of coal are considered to be negligible, because the plant is assumed to be mine-mouth. The module also includes the total emissions to air and water from the entire plant. Coke oven gas, tar, and benzene are byproducts of coking.

Name: Direct air capture system construction, solvent-based, 1MtCO2
Description:

Name: Hard coal, at mine
Description: Update 2022 by ZHAW only updated methane emissions at mine, Remark: Average data for coal mining in the specific region have been taken from a summary study on material flows and energy uses. Data are normalized by the mass unit of produced coal, including preparation and without differentiating steam coal from the rest. In order to enable a consistent calculation of the cumulative energy demand, the extracted mass of raw coal was adjusted by a factor of 1.03, taking into account the difference in the upper heating value of raw coal of this region (19.7 MJ/kg), compared to the used worldwide average of 19.1 MJ/kg. Mine reclamation is not included in this module, because it mostly concerns the tailings, which are described in a separate module. Electricity, heating from heavy oil industrial boilers, and diesel uses are included. The use of the module "heat, at hard coal industrial furnace 1-10MW" leads to an underestimation of emissions, because the quality of coal burned at mines is usually lower than coal burned in industrial boilers elsewhere. Electricity supply is modelled with the UCTE mix, because no specific mix has been modelled. Water uses in mining and coal washing have been approximately described using the module "tap water". Particle emissions are assumed to be all greater than 10 micrometer. Radon emissions are average value worldwide. Methane emissions are region specific. Emissions to water are estimated for Western European conditions and applied to this region. They are assumed to be released to rivers. Possible emissions to groundwater have not been accounted for. All coalbed methane released from the seam is accounted for as natural gas resource. However the recovered methane, possibly used for district heating and for energetic needs of some individual mines, has not been described as an energy byproduct. The unaccounted energy is nevertheless negligible compared to the energy content of the product coal (maximum of two percent for underground mining).; NA; UUID: ded61674-3634-439d-8f57-4fe923a032d8 includedProcesses:Included processes: The module represents average operational conditions in the relevant geographical region. It quantifies the directly affected area and occupation during operation of the mine. Electricity, heat, and diesel requirements for mining operation are included. Pumped groundwater, explosives, emissions to air and water, and solid waste complete the module. Not included is the methane recovered.

Description: Modeled is the operation of a plant fabricating UO2 fuel for light water nuclear reactors (PWR and BWR), with no MOX (mixed oxides), no RepU (reprocessed fuel), and no HEU (highly enriched uranium from warheads) fuel elements. Hence the radioactive emissions (and spectrum) as well as the radioactive solid waste may have been somewhat underestimated. Data for the operation of a nuclear fuel fabrication facility are relatively old but emissions to water are complete for a US plant. Radioactive emissions to air and water have been taken or derived from two commercial German facilities: both (one operational, the other closed) exhibit emissions per unit of product fuel much lower than data published in the 1980s. Name: Carbon dioxide, captured at municipal solid waste incineration plant, with heat recovery, for subsequent reuse
Description:
The MEA technology considered for this study is modelled after Tang and You, 2018, Reiter and Lindorfer, 2015. After flue gas condensation, the cooled flue gas is fed into a reactor containing a 30% MEA solution, which absorbs around 85â€“90% of the CO2, typically at 25 Â°Câ€“50 Â°C at 1 bar. The process is exothermic. The CO2-rich solution is heated afterwards to 100â€“140 Â°C, and in a stripper at 1â€“2 bars the CO2 desorbs from the MEA and leaves saturated with water vapour. The water is then condensed from the CO2 stream, and the CO2 is compressed to around 150 bar for transporting in pipes or a lower pressure for local tank storage and shipment by truck. The recovered MEA is reused in the plant (Pour et al., 2018). About 4 kg of MEA is used per tonne of CO2, due to degradation (releasing around 0.1 kg NH3 per tonne CO2 captured), the formation of heat-stable salts and losses as vapour and aerosols during stripping (the latter is around 0.01 kg per tonne of CO2 captured). NaOH is added in the stripping step at an amount of 0.1 kg per tonne CO2 captured. Around 4 kg of solid waste is generated per tonne of CO2 captured; this waste is disregarded. The MEA CC process also reduces the content of other pollutants in the flue gas, the extent of which depends on whether flue gas condensation is already in place or is introduced as part of the CO2 capture system. SOx, HCl, particulate matter and heavy metals are reduced to very low levels by flue gas condensation and subsequent CC. The level of NH3 increases in the flue gas after CC because of degradation of MEA. Here, an optimistic case of heat recovery is considered: 90% of the heat required by the capture plant is prvided by recovering heat from the flue gases of the MSWI plant. This is not included here. Source: Valentina Bisinella, Tore Hulgaard, Christian Riber, Anders Damgaard, Thomas H. Christensen, Environmental assessment of carbon capture and storage (CCS) as a post-treatment technology in waste incineration, Waste Management, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1/j.wasman0.20.040.05.

Name: Electrolyzer production, 1MWe, AEC, Stack

Name: Quarrying of olivine
Description:
"This dataset represents the supply of 1 kg of olivine. The authors assumed that an area of 200,000m2 will be mined over 50 years, with an annual capacity of 500 kt, i.e., 0.5 m2 for land use and 0.01 m2 per year for land use change are ascribed per FU. An average topsoil thickness of 0.2 m, with a bulk density of 1.3 t m−3, is considered, suggesting that 1.04 kt of overburden is produced year-round. For overburden handling, a bulldozer and a hydraulic shovel is considered, with the energy input taken from US Department of Energy, corresponding to activities in a surface limestone mine, whereas 200 km was ascribed for overburden transportation, used for backfilling. The quarry infrastructure was assumed to be similar to that of a gravel/sand quarry, as described in Kellenberger et al.
Source: Foteinis, S., Campbell, J. S., & Renforth, P. (2023). Life Cycle Assessment of Coastal Enhanced Weathering for Carbon Dioxide Removal from Air. Environmental Science and Technology, 57(15), 6169–6178. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.2c08633

****Additional comments****
Diesel, represents the diesel amount used for bulldozers and hydraulic shovel for overburden handling, for drilling, the diesel used for trucks, graders and lighting for mining operations and the energy input for loading. For the machinery used in quarrying (drill, service trucks, bulk trucks, and graders), Ecoinvent’s data for diesel burned in agricultural machinery, i.e., for running a tractor with a trailer, was used as a proxy.
The quarry infrastructure was assumed to be similar to that of a gravel/sand quarry, as described in Kellenberger et al.
For blasting, explosives consumption ranges from 0.145 kg (basalt) to 0.374 kg (granite) per extracted t, with the higher value considered herein since this leads to better fragmentation, which is beneficial for comminution.
Lubricating oil used for drilling and loading. For rock drilling, the lubricating oil consumption is considered as described in Rosado et al.
For water pumping, a mean energy of 0.45 kWh per m3 was ascribed for (borehole) water pumping (diesel-powered).

Name: Hydrogen production, gaseous, 100 bar, from methane pyrolysis
Description:
1 kg H2 produced by pyrolyzing methane. Pyrolysis processes decompose hydrocarbons into solid carbon and hydrogen at high temperatures (thermally or biologicalally). As no oxygen is present, no carbon oxides are formed, potentially eliminating the need for secondary processing steps such as the WGSR. The higher H2 concentration of the product gas stream also has considerable potential for minimising downstream clean-up processes. From a carbon-storage perspective, pyrolysis processes offer the advantage of storing a solid C-product as opposed to gaseous CO2. There is no alloc. of the process burden between the co-production of hydrogen and black carbon: the entirety of the burden is attributed to hydrogen production. Source: Amjad Al-Qahtani, Brett Parkinson, Klaus Hellgardt, Nilay Shah, Gonzalo Guillen-Gosalbez, Uncovering the true cost of hydrogen production routes using life cycle monetisation, Applied Energy, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1/j.apenergy0.20.12. The energy required is from DOI:10.1/ceat0.2. For pyrolysis, it can be provided both electrically and by burning some of the natural gas or pyrolysis products. For the comparison of technologies, electrical resistance heating is assumed, as use of this type of heating is deemed to be most practicable. The power requirement of 7.23 MWhel/ton H2 is based on thermodynamic calculations. These take into account both the energy losses during heat recovery and the compression power of 2 MWhel/ton H2, to compress pyrolysis hydrogen from 2 bar to 100 bar with three interim cooling stages. Inventories consolidated with numbers for infrastructures from Appendix A1 from Postels et al., 2016 https://doi.org/10.1/j.ijhydene0.20.090.17. Missing input of quartz for reactor, as unavailable in ecoinvent.

Name: Railway track, open field, single track
Description: The inventory contains the expenditure and material consumption for 1 km of open railway line, single-track. According to SBB (pers. communication, SBB, 2024), the open railway line consists of a railway embankment with a height of 3 m and an additional width of 5.2 m on both sides of the track bed. Data from the SCHIG report (SCHIG mbH, 2022) was used for the construction of the railway embankment. It was assumed that 70% of the soil for the railway embankment would have to be transported and that 30% of the material would be moved locally. The soil itself was not analysed (no production emissions). The ecoinvent standard values were used for the transport distances of the material deliveries. The track bed itself is 7 m wide for the single-track railway line. The sleepers are installed at a distance of 60cm. The rails are mounted on the sleepers, with 1 metre of rail weighing around 57 kg. The open railway line also requires a traction current system (masts, overhead lines) and a safety system.  The service life of an open railway line is 80 years, whereby the service life of the rails is 25 years and that of the sleepers 40 years. After that, refurbishment or new construction is due. Maintenance, refurbishment or dismantling were not taken into account in these inventories.; UUID:0b9e1f6e-f45a-4351-9984-4748c33c0d81 includedProcesses:The inventory includes all the materials, energy and transport necessary for constructing a railway single track on an open field. Excluded are maintenance and disposal
